CausalChain: Reduced serum albumin -> impaired binding and clearance of inflammatory mediators -> enhanced systemic and local inflammation -> promotion of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment -> diminished efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors; Conversely, interventions that increase albumin synthesis -> re-establishment of optimal albumin-bilirubin balance -> reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokines -> restoration of effective immune surveillance -> improved immunotherapy outcomes.
Hypothesis: Interventions aimed at increasing serum albumin levels to correct the albumin-bilirubin balance can remodel the HCC tumor microenvironment by reducing inflammation and immunosuppression, thereby enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Abstract: The ALBI grade, which integrates serum albumin and bilirubin levels, has been widely adopted as a prognostic tool for patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) across various treatment modalities. Although originally designed as a surrogate for hepatic reserve, emerging observations suggest that the determinants underlying the ALBI grade may also influence the tumor microenvironment and immunological landscape. In this context, we propose that alterations in albumin levels, beyond merely reflecting liver synthetic function, may actively contribute to modulation of systemic and local immune responses. This review introduces a novel perspective whereby the albumin‐bilirubin balance is postulated to affect not only patient prognosis but also the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors by influencing inflammatory cytokine profiles and immune cell functionality within the liver. Consequently, therapeutic strategies that restore or enhance albumin synthesis might improve the antitumor immune response in HCC.
